# TITLE LINUX SECURITY HANDBOOK # SUBTITLE 1. LINUX SECURITY FOUNDATIONS # BADGES PAGE 1 OF 20 # SECTION_HEADINGS - LINUX SECURITY LAYERS - USERS, PROCESSES, FILES, SERVICES, AND NETWORK BOUNDARIES - AUTHENTICATION VS AUTHORIZATION - LEAST PRIVILEGE - ATTACK SURFACE - DEFENSE IN DEPTH - SECURITY BASELINE VS ONGOING MONITORING # BODY_PARAGRAPHS STRONG LINUX SECURITY STARTS WITH UNDERSTANDING THE FUNDAMENTALS OF HOW SYSTEMS, USERS, PROCESSES, AND NETWORKS INTERACT. Linux security is built in multiple layers including the kernel, system services, filesystem, users, and network. Every component interacts. Securing each layer reduces risk across the entire system. Authentication verifies who you are. Authorization determines what you are allowed to do. Both must be configured correctly. Users, services, and processes should have only the minimum permissions required to perform their tasks. Limit access. Reduce risk. Any point that can be used to attack your system. Reduce exposed services, open ports, and unnecessary access to shrink the attack surface. No single control is perfect. Use multiple layers of security so that if one layer fails, other layers continue to protect the system. A strong baseline sets the foundation.
